title: India Warns Meta: No Safe Harbour Protection If Indian Laws Are Violated
excerpt: Government sources say the 'message has gone home' as New Delhi presses for tighter content moderation, child safety measures, and deepfake labeling across Meta's platforms.
body:
• India has warned Meta that safe harbour immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act is conditional and could be revoked if the company violates Indian law.
  • Government sources said the "message has gone home" following multiple rounds of high-level talks on child sexual abuse material, deepfakes, and content moderation.
  • Meta has pledged to enhance detection systems and comply with a three-hour takedown deadline for harmful content flagged by authorities.
  • The government is also examining WhatsApp's planned username feature across all messaging platforms over fraud and impersonation concerns.

India's government has explicitly warned Meta Platforms that safe harbour protection — the legal shield that protects social media companies from liability for user-generated content — is not guaranteed if the company violates Indian law, government sources said this week.

"No safe harbour if law violated; the message has gone home," sources told reporters, describing the outcome of sustained talks between New Delhi and Meta's leadership over content moderation failures, child safety lapses, and the handling of deepfakes on its platforms.

The warning marks the sharpest language yet from the Indian government in a confrontation that has stretched across six weeks and multiple rounds of high-level meetings.

A Confrontation Months in the Making

The standoff began in July when a BBC investigation found that Instagram's recommendation algorithm had been promoting videos containing child sexual abuse material. Paid advertisements on Instagram using terms like "rape video" and "child video" were allegedly directing users to Telegram channels where such content was on sale, prompting the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to order the immediate removal of all such ads and content.

https://x.com/ArvindJ35594964/status/2089615905349324977

The crisis deepened when Facebook briefly restricted a post by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in late July — an incident Meta later described as a "technical error." In early August, Meta's global team, including Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, was summoned to New Delhi for face-to-face meetings with IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg personally apologized to Indian government officials over child sexual abuse content and deepfakes on the company's platforms, according to multiple Indian media reports.

Three-Hour Takedown Deadline

A central demand from the Indian government has been a three-hour deadline for removing specified categories of harmful content after it is flagged — a significant tightening from the previous 36-hour window. The timeline applies to child sexual abuse material, deepfakes, misleading AI-generated content, and other material deemed harmful under India's evolving regulatory framework, according to Communications Today.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OTtYMXvqnxM

"We would like to understand from them as to why some of these things have not been working the way they are supposed to work, and what are the challenges."

— S. Krishnan, IT Secretary, Government of India

Meta has pledged to enhance its due diligence measures and outlined improvements to its moderation systems aimed at addressing risks posed by generative artificial intelligence. The government, however, has maintained that compliance will be judged by outcomes rather than assurances, and that Meta's proposed measures will be closely monitored.

Safe Harbour Under Threat

The safe harbour provision under Section 79 of India's Information Technology Act protects platforms from automatic liability for content posted by users — but the protection is conditional. Platforms must comply with Indian law, fulfill due diligence obligations, and remain neutral in how they handle content.

A parliamentary panel has separately questioned whether Meta's actions — particularly the restriction of the Prime Minister's post — are consistent with those neutrality requirements. Legal experts told Livemint that while blanket revocation of safe harbour would require legislative changes, the immunity can be lost on a content-specific basis if a platform abets unlawful activity or fails to act on government orders.

India is Meta's largest market by active monthly users: Facebook has more than 700 million users, Instagram over 550 million, and WhatsApp over 850 million in the country.

WhatsApp Usernames and Deepfake Labeling

Beyond child safety, the government has flagged concerns about WhatsApp's planned username feature, which would let users be contacted without sharing their phone number. Officials cited risks of increased fraud, phishing, impersonation, and digital arrest scams, and directed WhatsApp to pause the rollout pending government consultation. WhatsApp has agreed to defer the feature launch, sources said.

The government has also demanded that deepfakes and synthetically generated content carry clear labeling for users. Officials indicated that automated moderation systems alone may not be sufficient in sensitive cases and sought greater human review before takedown decisions are made. Content moderation decisions taken by teams outside India — without adequate understanding of Indian languages, cultural context, and regional sensitivities — were also flagged as a concern.

What's Next

Technical consultations between MeitY and Meta are expected to continue, with officials examining how the company's recommendation algorithms, automated moderation systems, and AI-driven detection tools operate in practice. The outcome will be closely watched by the global tech industry, as India's approach to platform accountability could set precedents for how other large democracies regulate social media companies.
nri_angle: The escalating standoff between India and Meta could reshape how Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp operate for over 2 billion Indian users including the global diaspora.
